# Refactoring notes: mutual TLS for the monitoring channel

The three preceding sections resolved all four root causes the detection
reports. This section repairs the one channel they broke, which the detection
cannot report: the Spring Boot Admin server is not reconstructed as a
microservice, so it has no model for the detection to judge.

The first section already declared the loss. The Customer Core's connector
became mutually authenticated, and the monitoring server kept polling its
actuator endpoints as an anonymous client, so the Customer Core rejected it:

```
Spring Boot Admin, /instances, before this change
    customer-core                    OFFLINE
    customer-management-backend      UP
    customer-self-service-backend    UP
    policy-management-backend        UP
```

The repair is entirely on the monitoring side. Nothing belonging to the four
root causes was touched: the Customer Core's connector, the broker's two
connectors and the gRPC endpoint are exactly as the preceding sections describe
them, and this change does not weaken any of them. Monitoring is a
service-to-service channel like any other, so it gets the same refactoring,
**Use Mutual TLS**, rather than an exception carved out of the Customer Core.

## What changed

### The monitoring server: Spring Boot Admin

`spring-boot-admin/src/main/java/com/lakesidemutual/springbootadmin/MonitoringTlsConfiguration.java`
(new)

Spring Boot Admin polls the registered applications through an
`InstanceWebClient`, which its `AdminServerInstanceWebClientConfiguration`
builds from the `WebClient.Builder` bean Spring Boot auto-configures. The new
class contributes a `WebClientCustomizer` to that builder which replaces the
connector with a `JdkClientHttpConnector` over a `java.net.http.HttpClient`
carrying an `SSLContext` built from two stores: the key store with the
monitoring server's own certificate and private key, and the shared trust store
with the development CA.

The customizer is `@Order(Ordered.LOWEST_PRECEDENCE)` so that it runs after
Spring Boot's own `webClientHttpConnectorCustomizer`, whose connector it is
meant to replace.

`SSLContext` is handed to the JDK's `HttpClient` and nothing else is set, so
the client's default certificate-path and hostname verification stay in place.
This mirrors the two `RestTemplate` callers of the Customer Core, which use the
same JDK HTTP client through `JdkClientHttpRequestFactory`.

One connector serves every registered application, so the three services still
reached over plaintext HTTP are unaffected: an `http://` URL never enters the
TLS path.

`spring-boot-admin/src/main/resources/application.properties`

Four new properties, plus two optional `...Type` properties defaulting to
`PKCS12`, following the naming of `customercore.tls.*` in the three callers so
that the environment-variable override mechanism works the same way
(`MONITORING_TLS_KEYSTORE` and friends):

```properties
monitoring.tls.keyStore=file:./certs/spring-boot-admin.p12
monitoring.tls.keyStorePassword=changeit
monitoring.tls.trustStore=file:./certs/truststore.p12
monitoring.tls.trustStorePassword=changeit
```

### The other end: the Customer Core's registration

`customer-core/src/main/resources/application.properties`

```properties
spring.boot.admin.client.instance.service-base-url = https://localhost:8110
```

The scheme was never the problem. Spring Boot Admin's client derives it from
`server.ssl.enabled` (`DefaultApplicationFactory#getScheme`), so the Customer
Core had been registering `https://.../actuator` ever since its connector was
changed. The host was the problem: the same class derives it from
`InetAddress.getLocalHost().getHostName()`, which on the machine this was
verified on is `x37.clients.idial.fh` and is not a subject alternative name of
any certificate in this system. The monitoring server would reach the right
socket and then correctly refuse the certificate it was shown.

Pinning the registered base URL to a name the certificate carries is the fix.
It is the registration, not the connector: the connector, its port and its
`client-auth=need` are untouched. The three plaintext services were left alone;
they register under the same machine hostname and are reached over `http`,
where no hostname check applies.

### Certificates

`generate-certificates.sh` gained `spring-boot-admin` as a seventh service, so
it now issues a key store for it from the same development CA and copies it,
with the shared trust store, into `spring-boot-admin/certs/`. The script is
committed, its output is not, and `certs/` was already in `.gitignore`.

### Docker Compose

`docker-compose.yml` mounts `./spring-boot-admin/certs` read-only at `/certs`
for the monitoring server, the same way the other services receive theirs, and
passes `SPRING_BOOT_ADMIN_CLIENT_INSTANCE_SERVICE_BASE_URL=https://customer-core:8110`
to the Customer Core, that being the subject alternative name its certificate
carries inside the Compose network.

### Documentation

`README.md`, `FAQ.md` and `spring-boot-admin/README.md` were updated: the
monitoring server now appears among the components that need generated
material, the Spring Boot Admin README shows the `curl` invocation that reaches
the Customer Core's actuator endpoints, and the FAQ has an entry for
"Spring Boot Admin shows the Customer Core as OFFLINE".

## What was assumed

- **The monitoring server degrades rather than refusing to start.** When the
  stores are absent, the bean logs a `WARN` naming both paths and the script
  that produces them, and contributes no customizer. The server then starts,
  monitors the three plaintext services, and leaves the Customer Core
  `OFFLINE`. The alternative — failing startup — was rejected because
  monitoring should not be able to take the system down, and because the
  monitoring server has no test suite, so a hard failure would surface only at
  run time anyway. Nothing is trusted that would not otherwise be trusted: the
  fallback is the stock JDK client with the stock trust store and no client
  certificate, not a permissive one.
- **The monitoring server has an identity of its own.** It gets its own
  certificate rather than borrowing another service's, for the same reason the
  Risk Management Client got one: mutual TLS exists to authenticate peers.
- **The monitoring server's own connector stays plaintext HTTP on port 9000**,
  and so does the registration direction, in which the four services POST to
  it. Securing that direction would mean turning the admin UI and
  `http://localhost:9000/instances` into HTTPS, which is a different channel,
  outside the scope this repair was given, and would break the stated
  acceptance check. It is a real remaining plaintext channel and is listed
  below as such.
- **`WebClientCustomizer` rather than Spring Boot's SSL bundles.**
  `spring.ssl.bundle.jks.*` with `WebClientSsl` would be fewer lines, but a
  bundle is loaded eagerly at context refresh and throws when the store file is
  missing, which rules out the graceful degradation above. The hand-built
  `SSLContext` also matches what the three callers of the Customer Core already
  do.
- **Password and validity** are unchanged from the earlier sections:
  `changeit`, 365 days, development only.

## What was verified

All five Spring Boot applications were started from their own directories with
`./mvnw spring-boot:run` against freshly generated material.

- `http://localhost:9000/instances` reports **four services, all `UP`**, with
  the Customer Core registered as `https://localhost:8110/`:

  ```
  policy-management-backend        UP   http://x37.clients.idial.fh:8090/
  customer-self-service-backend    UP   http://x37.clients.idial.fh:8080/
  customer-management-backend      UP   http://x37.clients.idial.fh:8100/
  customer-core                    UP   https://localhost:8110/
  ```

- The Customer Core's request log shows the poll arriving over the TLS
  connector every 20 seconds, from the JDK client the new configuration
  installs:

  ```
  DEBUG ... CommonsRequestLoggingFilter : Before request [GET /actuator/health,
      headers=[... host:"localhost:8110", user-agent:"Java-http-client/21.0.12.1", ...]]
  ```

- **Negative: no client certificate.** A request to
  `https://localhost:8110/actuator/health` that trusts the development CA but
  presents no certificate is rejected during the handshake with
  `tlsv13 alert certificate required`. The same request presenting
  `spring-boot-admin.crt.pem` and its key returns `200 {"status":"UP"}`. The
  Customer Core's connector therefore still requires a client certificate, and
  the monitoring server reaches it by presenting one, not because anything was
  relaxed.
- **Clean checkout, no key material.** With every `certs/` directory deleted,
  `./mvnw -B test` passes in `spring-boot-admin` (no tests, build succeeds) and
  in `customer-core` (26 tests, 0 failures). The monitoring server starts in
  that state and logs the expected warning:

  ```
  WARN c.l.s.MonitoringTlsConfiguration : No key or trust store found at
      URL [file:certs/spring-boot-admin.p12] and URL [file:certs/truststore.p12] ...
  ```

- `git status` is clean of generated key material: `certs/`, `*.p12`, `*.jks`
  and `*.csr` were already ignored, and the new `spring-boot-admin/certs/`
  falls under the same `certs/` rule.
- No test was disabled and no assertion was weakened. No
  `TrustAllStrategy`, `NoopHostnameVerifier`, `InsecureTrustManagerFactory` or
  `rejectUnauthorized: false` appears anywhere in the patch.

## What could not be verified, and known consequences

- **The reconstruction and the detection were not re-run.** The toolchain is
  not present in this worktree and the instructions are to stay inside it.
  Reasoning only: no plaintext address was introduced by this change. The one
  property added to a modelled service,
  `spring.boot.admin.client.instance.service-base-url`, carries `https`; the
  pre-existing `spring.boot.admin.client.url = http://localhost:9000` in all
  four services is untouched and produced no finding before.
- **The Docker Compose deployment was not started.** Verification ran the
  services directly on the host. The Compose changes are a volume mount of the
  same shape the other services already have and one environment variable, but
  the containerised path was not exercised.
- **`kubernetes/manifests/` and `kubernetes/docker-compose.yml` were not
  updated**, and the monitoring server will not reach the Customer Core there.
  Changing Kubernetes manifests was ruled out for this work.
- **The registration direction is still plaintext.** The four services POST
  their registration to `http://spring-boot-admin:9000`, and the admin UI is
  served over plaintext HTTP. That is a genuine remaining non-secured channel.
  It is outside the scope this repair was given, and the acceptance check for
  it is stated in terms of `http://localhost:9000/instances`, so it was left
  alone deliberately rather than overlooked.
- **The registered address is now pinned**, which means a developer who reaches
  the Customer Core under some other name has to override
  `SPRING_BOOT_ADMIN_CLIENT_INSTANCE_SERVICE_BASE_URL` and add that name to the
  certificate's subject alternative names in `generate-certificates.sh`.
- **No authorisation beyond the channel.** Any holder of a certificate from the
  development CA can read the Customer Core's actuator endpoints. §3.7 is about
  the channel; endpoint authorisation would be a separate refactoring.
- **Windows.** Unchanged from the earlier sections: `generate-certificates.sh`
  is a bash script with no `.bat` equivalent.

## What changed

**`spring-boot-admin/.../MonitoringTlsConfiguration.java`** (new) — a `WebClientCustomizer` at `LOWEST_PRECEDENCE` that replaces the connector on the auto-configured `WebClient.Builder` (the one SBA's `AdminServerInstanceWebClientConfiguration` builds its `InstanceWebClient` from) with a `JdkClientHttpConnector` over a `java.net.http.HttpClient` carrying an `SSLContext` from the admin server's own key store plus the shared trust store. One connector serves every instance, so the three plaintext services are untouched — an `http://` URL never enters the TLS path. Defaults for path and hostname verification are left alone.

**`customer-core/.../application.properties`** — `spring.boot.admin.client.instance.service-base-url = https://localhost:8110`. The *scheme* was never wrong (SBA's client derives it from `server.ssl.enabled`), but the *host* was: `DefaultApplicationFactory` uses `InetAddress.getLocalHost().getHostName()`, which here is `x37.clients.idial.fh` and is in no certificate's SANs. The connector, its port and `client-auth=need` are untouched.

**`generate-certificates.sh`** — `spring-boot-admin` added as a seventh service. **`docker-compose.yml`** — certs mount for the admin server, Compose-name base URL for the Customer Core. **README/FAQ/spring-boot-admin README** updated, and the fourth section of `REFACTORING-NOTES.md` records the change, the assumptions and the gaps.

## Verified

- All five Spring Boot services started; `http://localhost:9000/instances` reports **four services, all `UP`**, Customer Core as `https://localhost:8110/`.
- Customer Core's request log shows the poll arriving on the TLS connector from `Java-http-client/21.0.12.1` every 20s.
- Negative: an HTTPS request to `/actuator/health` trusting the CA but presenting no client certificate is rejected with `tlsv13 alert certificate required`; the same request with `spring-boot-admin.crt.pem` returns `200 {"status":"UP"}`. The connector was not relaxed.
- Clean checkout with every `certs/` deleted: `./mvnw -B test` passes in `spring-boot-admin` and `customer-core` (26 tests, 0 failures), and the admin server starts with a `WARN` naming the missing stores and the script. No key material is tracked by git.

## Not verified

- **Detection was not re-run** — MRF isn't in this worktree and I stayed inside it. Reasoning only: the single property added to a modelled service carries `https`; the pre-existing `spring.boot.admin.client.url = http://localhost:9000` is unchanged and produced no finding before.
- Docker Compose was not started; Kubernetes manifests were deliberately not touched, so the monitoring channel stays broken there.
- **The registration direction is still plaintext** — the four services POST to `http://spring-boot-admin:9000` and the UI is HTTP. Securing it would contradict the stated acceptance check (`http://localhost:9000/instances`), so I left it and flagged it in the notes rather than silently widening scope.

One judgement call worth your attention: when the stores are absent the admin server logs a warning and falls back to the stock JDK client rather than failing startup — monitoring shouldn't be able to take the system down, and it has no test suite to catch a hard failure. Nothing permissive is installed in that path.
